Jesus said to his disciples, "Assuredly I say to you that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. And again, I say to you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God." So, as I keep on telling you, Jesus himself was very anti-rich. He believed that the rich people, because they were too focused on material acquisitions, could never go into heaven.

The paradox is that the Catholic Church becomes extremely wealthy. If you visit St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican, it is one of the most beautiful buildings in the world and is still among the wealthiest organizations in history. The wealth accumulated by the Vatican was possible because Western Europe started to become very wealthy from about 1000 to 1300 due to technological innovation, a warming climate that allowed for better agriculture, the rise of cities, and increased trade with other regions.

During this period, Europe's population doubled, making the Catholic Church much more powerful than the empire. The emperor was human and could change his mind or make poor decisions, whereas the church's authority came from God, who was seen as perfect, immutable, and eternal. Thus, the church demanded not just labor but souls, and its power to send people to hell for eternity made it an even more potent force.

The church established a strict hierarchy where priests spoke in Latin, which most people could not understand, and only a select few were allowed to read the Bible due to illiteracy. The rituals of the Catholic Church included practices like the Eucharist, where believers believe they are eating the body and blood of Jesus through transubstantiation. This divine bureaucracy could determine who went to heaven or hell and for how long.

The church's power was so great that it could excommunicate kings, effectively removing them from the Christian community and allowing other rulers to kill them with impunity. The Catholic Church's wealth also led to corruption, as its leaders used their position to enrich themselves through practices like indulgences, which allowed rich people to buy forgiveness for sins.

In summary, while Jesus was anti-rich, the Catholic Church became extremely wealthy due to historical circumstances and its powerful bureaucracy, leading to both its success and inherent corruption.
